message.content: {"angles":[{"local_key":"reviews_vs_buyer_research","title":"Great reviews are not the same as knowing why people chose you","content_opportunity":"Whitney says that when she asks full-service clients about market research, the usual answer is \"check out our reviews.\" She separates praise from direct research: asking a new client, soon after they sign, what actually decided it for them. The answers can then shape the ads and messaging. The piece would use this exchange to show the difference between happy-client evidence and buying-decision evidence.","strategic_purpose":"WARM","content_type":"thought_shift","strategic_rationale":"It shows how WIA thinks about messaging and positioning as research-led work, ahead of keywords and targeting. That builds trust with established owners who already have strong reviews and want their marketing to connect with buyers.","audience":"Established wedding venues and pros with good reviews who assume testimonials already tell them how couples decide, and who want their ads and messaging to speak to real buying triggers.","core_perspective":"Reviews show that clients were happy. They do not show what tipped a couple into choosing you, and only that second answer tells you what your ads should say.","tension":"Owners with glowing reviews can feel they already know their buyers, yet nobody has asked the newest clients what made them say yes.","wia_expertise_in_action":"Whitney draws on what she hears when onboarding full-service clients, separates reviews from decision-factor research, and recommends a short post-signing survey in LeadLock so both the client and WIA see the answers and can feed them into the advertising strategy.","service_relevance":"The survey was proposed for this client inside LeadLock. Current LeadLock survey capabilities and scope should be verified before any public mention.","reader_decision":null,"evidence_readiness":"supported","research_questions":[],"selection_reason":"The distinction between praise and decision-factor evidence is a clear, transferable belief with a concrete method behind it, and it does not repeat the existing Reel examples. It gives owners a new way to question what they think they know about their buyers.","moment_ids":["moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6"],"source_assertions":["[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Whitney said that when onboarding full-service clients she often asks whether they have market research, and that the usual response is that they have great reviews.","[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Whitney distinguished reviews from market research, describing research as asking a new client why they signed and what their deciding factors were.","[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Whitney said those answers could be layered back into ad or marketing strategy, and offered to create a market research survey in LeadLock for both of the client's offerings, sent about a week after a client signs.","[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Whitney said both the client and WIA would see the responses, and described the aim as learning buying triggers so the ads can attract more of the right people.","[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Mike said it was a great idea and Marisa said she would do it."],"inference":"Reviews and decision-factor research answer different questions, and treating one as a substitute for the other leaves a gap in messaging strategy.","qualifiers":["The survey was proposed. It had not been drafted, approved or sent in this exchange.","Whitney's observation that this happens \"across the board\" is her experience, not a measured prevalence.","That the research will attract more of the right people is Whitney's rationale, not a measured result.","Speaker labels are unverified."],"risks":["The client's businesses are identifiable in the transcript, so anonymize and check consent before using the scene.","Verify current LeadLock survey features before implying a capability.","Do not present any survey findings, because none exist in this source."],"quality":{"grounding":4.5,"strategic_fit":4.5,"distinctiveness":4.0,"audience_resonance":4.0,"source_strength":4.2,"reasons":["The distinction is stated plainly by Whitney and accepted by both clients, with a concrete method described.","It is a thought shift with a clear audience stake and requires no outcome claim.","No historical comparison is available, so novelty is not asserted beyond the existing Reel examples, which do not cover this."]}},{"local_key":"two_forms_two_questions","title":"Why the question of why they chose you and the question of what the musician should know belong in different forms","content_opportunity":"Two clients wanted to learn more about their couples: one for marketing (what attracted buyers) and one for service (so musicians feel connected to the couple's story). When Marisa asked about folding both into one comprehensive pre-wedding form, Whitney recommended two separate tools with different timing, length and systems. The piece would show how one set of client knowledge serves two jobs.","strategic_purpose":"WARM","content_type":"process","strategic_rationale":"It shows WIA's practical reasoning about research design and how marketing intelligence differs from service operations. That supports authority without a hard sell.","audience":"Wedding businesses with a team of performers or vendors who want to know more about their couples, both to sell better and to deliver a more personal day.","core_perspective":"Learning why someone bought and preparing to serve them are different questions. They are best asked at different moments, in different forms, for different readers.","tension":"It is tempting to ask everything in one form, but a short, timely buying-decision survey and a thorough wedding-day planning form do different jobs.","wia_expertise_in_action":"Whitney recommended a short research survey (about five questions, mostly multiple choice, one or two open-ended) sent within days to a week of signing, while the buying decision is fresh. She put it in LeadLock and recommended a separate pre-wedding planning form in the client's CRM that can be shared with the performers.","service_relevance":"LeadLock is proposed as the home for the research survey. The scope and capabilities are described only by Whitney's proposal and should be verified.","reader_decision":null,"evidence_readiness":"supported","research_questions":[],"selection_reason":"It captures the client contribution (Marisa's performer-connection need, Mike's curiosity about what attracted buyers) and Whitney's translation of those needs into two distinct tools. It is a different central idea from the reviews-versus-research angle.","moment_ids":["moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1"],"source_assertions":["[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Marisa said it would help the DJs to know more about the couple, such as a meaningful detail that makes performers feel part of the couple's story.","[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Mike said it would be interesting to learn what attracted buyers, for example the saxophonist or the lighting.","[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Marisa asked whether the questions should go out from LeadLock or be added to a revamped, more comprehensive wedding info form.","[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Whitney said she would treat them as two separate things. She recommended a market research survey sent a couple of days to a week after signing, with about five questions, mostly multiple choice, built in LeadLock.","[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Whitney recommended a separate pre-wedding planning form in the client's CRM for wedding-day needs that could be shared with musicians or the band.","[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Marisa said she could paste the survey link into the existing welcome flow, and Whitney confirmed the survey would be built in LeadLock and could be emailed from anywhere."],"inference":"Separating the two purposes keeps the research short and well timed, while letting the operational form be as thorough as the team needs.","qualifiers":["All of this is a proposal. Completion, welcome-flow placement and resulting insights are not established.","The suggested benefits for musicians and examples of what attracted buyers came from the clients, not from survey findings.","Speaker labels are unverified."],"risks":["The clients and their offerings are identifiable, so anonymize and check consent.","Do not present performer-matching or personalization benefits as delivered or measured.","Verify LeadLock capabilities before mentioning them."],"quality":{"grounding":4.3,"strategic_fit":4.0,"distinctiveness":3.6,"audience_resonance":3.6,"source_strength":4.2,"reasons":["Both client needs and Whitney's recommendation are clearly stated.","The idea shares the survey context with the reviews angle but has a different central point, which is separation of purposes.","The exchange is planned work with no outcome, which limits strength but does not undermine the process lesson."]}},{"local_key":"attribution_vs_big_picture","title":"What attribution can't see: the couple who clicks an ad now and inquires on their own two weeks later","content_opportunity":"In a strategy call, the clients' business was reported as up about 30% year to date, while WIA's attribution data covers only inquiries that came through ads. Whitney explained how an ad can influence someone who inquires organically later, and that it is worth checking the ads in isolation and also whether the whole business is improving. She also proposed adding actual sales figures to reports, not just booked calls.","strategic_purpose":"WARM","content_type":"thought_shift","strategic_rationale":"Owners are often unsure what ad reports can and cannot show. This frames WIA as honest about attribution limits and focused on business-level outcomes, which builds trust with owners who are skeptical of ad reporting.","audience":"Wedding business owners evaluating their ads who either credit only tracked leads or struggle to connect ad reports to overall business growth.","core_perspective":"Attribution data tells you what came through the ads. It does not tell you everything the ads influenced, so check that the ads work in isolation and also that the whole business is moving.","tension":"Some bookings, such as planner referrals, arrive with no known source, and some leads say they saw the business on Instagram without anyone knowing whether it was an ad.","wia_expertise_in_action":"Whitney proposed adding sales figures to reports and having Carmen pull the January to April sales history. She also explained the ad-then-organic customer journey and why direct attribution and overall performance give different information.","service_relevance":"Reporting that includes sales data is proposed for this client. The format and scope of reporting should not be assumed to apply to other clients.","reader_decision":null,"evidence_readiness":"supported","research_questions":[],"selection_reason":"It exposes a real boundary in interpreting ad results without dismissing attribution data or the client's broader context. The scene includes the client's own uncertainty, which makes the principle credible.","moment_ids":["moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711"],"source_assertions":["[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Whitney said reports would include actual sales, not just booked calls, and said Carmen had found that one Google Ads lead in May turned into a $14,000 booking for the client's higher-priced offering.","[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Whitney said that one May booking covered everything spent on ads that year, and gave a rough ROI of about 7x with \"something like that.\"","[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Mike said the accountant and bookkeeper indicated the business was up about 30% year to date.","[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Whitney said the reports show leads attributed to ads, but that ads can have an impact not visible in attribution data, describing someone who clicks an ad, researches the business, and inquires organically a week or two later.","[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Mike said some bookings are not in LeadLock because planners contact him directly, and he does not know how those clients found the business. Whitney raised that planners may have seen ads.","[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Marisa said callers almost always say they think they saw the business on Instagram, which she assumed must be an ad."],"inference":"Ad-attributed results and overall business movement answer different questions, and treating either as the whole picture is misleading.","qualifiers":["The $14,000 booking is reported in the meeting. There is no independent verification or collected-revenue detail, and the cost basis for the claim that it covers ad spend was not stated.","The 7x figure was an off-the-cuff estimate and should not be used as a result.","The 30% increase was attributed to the accountant and bookkeeper. Its period and calculation were not detailed, and it is not attributed to ads.","Whitney's ad-to-organic journey is a possible explanation, not a demonstration for the untracked planner bookings.","Marisa's Instagram comments were anecdotal and did not establish whether callers saw organic content or an ad.","Speaker labels are unverified."],"risks":["Do not claim ads caused the 30% growth or the untracked bookings.","Do not publish the $14,000 or 7x figures without verification and client consent.","The clients are identifiable, so check privacy and consent.","Do not generalize the planner-referral situation to other businesses."],"quality":{"grounding":4.3,"strategic_fit":4.5,"distinctiveness":4.0,"audience_resonance":4.4,"source_strength":4.3,"reasons":["The attribution boundary and the client's own uncertainty are clearly preserved in the source.","The perspective is a trust-building principle that does not depend on a verified result.","Several strong figures in the source carry weak verification, so the angle deliberately does not depend on them."]}},{"local_key":"quiet_niche_campaign","title":"A niche ad campaign with almost no clicks: what to watch before you turn it off","content_opportunity":"A photographer's senior-photo search campaign had only about 10 monthly searches in her local area, and even after broadening the terms it got impressions but no clicks. Carmen reasoned that with no clicks there is no click cost, so leaving it running was low-risk and might catch a back-to-school spike. The signal to reassess is clicks without leads. The piece would show how low demand, timing, and campaign behavior shaped a bounded test.","strategic_purpose":"WARM","content_type":"education","strategic_rationale":"It gives owners with a smaller side service a more useful way to think about a quiet campaign than \"keep it\" or \"kill it.\" That demonstrates measured, honest advisory judgment.","audience":"Wedding business owners running or considering ads for a smaller service, a secondary offer, or a limited local market.","core_perspective":"A campaign with little search demand and no clicks isn't costing much. The one to worry about is the one getting clicks without leads.","tension":"It's uncomfortable to keep an ad running that isn't producing anything, but stopping may mean missing a seasonal window you can't see yet.","wia_expertise_in_action":"Carmen explained the low search volume and the broadened keywords, asked when inquiries usually arrive, said click costs are not incurred without clicks, named clicks without leads as the trigger to reconsider, and suggested a visual Meta test. Whitney guessed that back-to-school could bring more traction.","service_relevance":null,"reader_decision":null,"evidence_readiness":"supported","research_questions":[],"selection_reason":"It shows a concrete decision rule from an expert, shaped by the client's own knowledge of her inquiry volume, and ends with an open test rather than a claim of success.","moment_ids":["moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259"],"source_assertions":["[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Carmen said the senior-photos campaign had very low search volume, about 10 searches a month on average for her keywords in the local area, and that she broadened the targeting to anything senior-related but still got impressions and no clicks.","[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Bri said senior inquiries are not high volume, probably fewer than 10 a month and fairly stable, and wondered whether the season mattered.","[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Carmen said she did not think it hurt to keep it running, and Bri said she doesn't pay unless people click.","[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Carmen said a spike might come around the start of school in August or September, and that the only problem with keeping a campaign on is getting clicks and no leads, which would be a waste of money.","[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Carmen suggested that if Bri ran Meta, senior photos might do well on Instagram. Whitney guessed there may be more traction with back to school."],"inference":"The decision is about spending exposure and a plausible seasonal window, not a blanket rule for when to keep or stop a campaign.","qualifiers":["The seasonal increase is a hypothesis, not an observed trend.","The campaign's later results are not reported.","Search volume and inquiry numbers are specific to this business and area.","Management time or fees were not discussed, so \"costs nothing\" applies only to click spend.","Speaker labels are unverified."],"risks":["The location and client are identifiable, so anonymize and avoid naming the local area.","Do not present the keep-it-running decision as a universal recommendation.","Avoid stating that the campaign worked."],"quality":{"grounding":4.4,"strategic_fit":3.8,"distinctiveness":3.8,"audience_resonance":3.6,"source_strength":4.0,"reasons":["The decision, its conditions and the client's contribution are all visible in the source.","It relies on no outcome claim and states clear limits.","The audience is narrower, since it concerns a smaller secondary service."]}},{"local_key":"creative_refresh_by_performance","title":"New ad creative every month doesn't mean swapping out the ads that are working","content_opportunity":"When Marisa asked how often ads are refreshed, Carmen said new creatives are produced monthly but that she generally avoids changing what is working, refreshes retargeting about every two months, and refreshes conversion campaigns more when performance is declining. Marisa then asked for a formal review cadence so she wouldn't miss updates. The piece would explore refreshing on performance rather than on a calendar.","strategic_purpose":"WARM","content_type":"process","strategic_rationale":"It shows the reasoning behind a common agency practice and gives owners a way to evaluate creative-refresh claims, which builds trust and authority.","audience":"Owners running ads who assume fresh creative should replace old creative on a fixed schedule, or who wonder how involved they should be in reviewing campaign work.","core_perspective":"Make new creative regularly, but let performance decide what gets replaced, because changing a campaign that is working carries its own risk.","tension":"Owners want to know that work is being done, while an ad that is performing may be best left alone.","wia_expertise_in_action":"Carmen explained that she leaves working creative largely alone because changes can affect the algorithm, refreshes retargeting about every two months, and refreshed one client's conversion campaigns more often when performance declined. Whitney offered a recurring strategy meeting.","service_relevance":"A recurring strategy meeting was offered to this client. Monthly creative and meeting cadence should not be treated as a standard WIA deliverable without verification.","reader_decision":null,"evidence_readiness":"supported","research_questions":[],"selection_reason":"It pairs a clear expert trade-off with a client-led adjustment to how work is reviewed, and it is distinct from the diagnostic and attribution angles.","moment_ids":["moment_baa14f0096a2495fb5aa0669"],"source_assertions":["[moment_baa14f0096a2495fb5aa0669] Marisa asked how often the ads are refreshed and how the content works.","[moment_baa14f0096a2495fb5aa0669] Carmen said there are new ad creatives each month and that she needs to send the new content monthly so there is a bank of approved creatives.","[moment_baa14f0096a2495fb5aa0669] Carmen said that if something is working she normally does not change it much because that can affect the algorithm, and that she refreshes retargeting campaigns maybe once every two months.","[moment_baa14f0096a2495fb5aa0669] Carmen said she refreshed one client's conversion campaigns more because performance was declining, so refresh timing depends on performance.","[moment_baa14f0096a2495fb5aa0669] Marisa said she sometimes misses the updates and wanted to set a formal meeting to review them. Whitney offered to turn the occasional monthly strategy meeting into a recurring one, and Marisa said that would be great."],"inference":"Refresh decisions weigh the risk of disturbing a working campaign against declining performance, and a structured review gives the owner a regular way to see the work.","qualifiers":["Carmen's explanation is her approach in this exchange, not a universal performance rule, and the algorithm effect is her account.","It is not established whether the recurring meeting was scheduled or helped.","The platform for the creative discussion is not specified.","Speaker labels are unverified."],"risks":["Do not present monthly creative or recurring meetings as a guaranteed WIA service.","The client's missed updates are a client-specific communication gap, so keep the focus on the principle.","Do not claim the algorithm effect as a verified fact."],"quality":{"grounding":4.2,"strategic_fit":3.9,"distinctiveness":3.6,"audience_resonance":3.8,"source_strength":4.0,"reasons":["Carmen's rationale and the client's review request are both stated clearly.","The algorithm claim is Carmen's account and limits strength.","It is a useful principle, but a less dramatic one than the attribution or diagnostic angles."]}},{"local_key":"slowdown_both_channels","title":"When inquiries slow down, the first question is whether it's only the ads","content_opportunity":"A venue client told Fallon her leads had slowed. Fallon asked whether she was seeing it organically too, then checked LeadLock and found both ads and organic had gone quiet. The client wanted to focus on more specific locations, which Fallon applied to Google targeting, and the client edited her landing page. A burst of leads followed, then another lull. The piece would show how to diagnose a slowdown across channels while keeping combined changes and unresolved causes honest.","strategic_purpose":"WARM","content_type":"process","strategic_rationale":"It shows WIA's practitioners diagnosing a problem with the client rather than defending the ads, and it models honest uncertainty. That builds trust with owners who have had ad reports blamed or credited without explanation.","audience":"Venue and wedding pro owners who notice a drop in inquiries and aren't sure whether to blame their ads, the season, or something else.","core_perspective":"Before changing a campaign, find out whether the slowdown is limited to paid ads or shows up everywhere, then look at targeting and the landing experience with the client.","tension":"A burst of leads after a change feels like proof, but the same pattern can return, and two changes at once make it hard to know which one mattered.","wia_expertise_in_action":"Fallon asked whether the slowdown also appeared organically and verified it in LeadLock. She applied the client's more specific locations to Google targeting and identified the ads or the page as the remaining suspects, reasoning that leads were not failing to book tours. She also planned to look further back at historical trends.","service_relevance":null,"reader_decision":null,"evidence_readiness":"supported","research_questions":[],"selection_reason":"The diagnostic question changes the scope of the problem, and the scene keeps the client's contribution, the team's actions and the unresolved recurrence distinct. The piece would use the visible review to show why a before-and-after read is more complicated than it looks.","strategic_purpose":"WARM","content_type":"campaign_breakdown","strategic_rationale":"It shows how a WIA practitioner checks evidence in front of the client, corrects herself, and stays cautious about a good-looking trend.
